en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
7. The Training Rule on Building Monasteries At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Now at that time, a householder who was a supporter of the Venerable Channa said this to the Venerable Channa:
“Venerable sir, please find a site for a monastery; we will have a dwelling built for you.

Then, while the Venerable Channa was clearing the site for the monastery, he had a certain sacred tree cut down—one that was honored by the village, honored by the town, honored by the city, honored by the district, and honored by the kingdom.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, have a shrine-tree cut down—one honored by the village, honored by the town, honored by the city, honored by the district, and honored by the kingdom?
The recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are harming a living being with a single sense-faculty!
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and spreading it about.
Those monks who were of few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the venerable Channa have a shrine-tree that is honored by the village … [as before] … honored by the kingdom, cut down?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Channa in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before].
“Is it true, Channa, that you had the shrine-tree—which was honored by the village, honored by the district, and honored by the kingdom—cut down?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How can you, foolish man, have a shrine-tree cut down—one honored by the village, honored by the town, honored by the city, honored by the district, and honored by the kingdom?
For people, foolish man, perceive life in a tree.
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on]."
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“When a monk is having a large dwelling built for himself that has an owner, he should bring monks along for the purpose of inspecting the site.
Those monks must designate a site that is free from harm and possesses space on all sides.”

"If a monk should have a large dwelling built on a site that is crowded and lacks space for circumambulation, and he does not have other monks approve the selection of the site, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A "large" dwelling is said to be one that has an owner.
A "vihāra" means it is either plastered on the inside, or plastered on the outside, or plastered both inside and outside.
"By one who is having it built" means...
Whether doing it oneself or causing another to do it.
"With an owner" means there is some other owner, whether a woman or a man, a householder or one who has gone forth.
"Attuddesaṃ" means for one's own benefit.
"Bhikkhus should be brought forward for the designation of the site" means that monks must be invited to designate the location.
That monk who is building a dwelling, having cleared the site for the dwelling, should approach the Saṅgha,
arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the elder monks, sit down on his haunches,
raise his joined palms, and speak as follows:
“Venerable sir, I wish to have a large dwelling built for myself, with a patron and dedicated to me personally.
Therefore, venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the dwelling.
It should be requested a second time as well.
It should be requested a third time as well.
If the entire Saṅgha is able to inspect the site for the monastery, it should be inspected by the entire Saṅgha.
If the entire Saṅgha is not able to inspect the site for the monastery, [it should be done by a group].

Those monks there who are experienced and competent to know whether a site involves harm or is free from harm, and whether it has space on all sides or lacks such space, should be requested and appointed. And thus, monks, they should be appointed: An experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha: “Monks, listen to me. If it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint such-and-such a monk as the site-designator for the purpose of designating the site for the hut-dwelling. This is the motion. “Listen, venerable sirs, to my words. The Saṅgha appoints such-and-such a monk as the site-designator for the purpose of designating the site for the hut-dwelling. Let those venerable ones who agree to appoint such-and-such a monk as the site-designator for the purpose of designating the site for the hut-dwelling remain silent; let those who do not agree speak. Such-and-such a monk has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the site-designator for the purpose of designating the site for the hut-dwelling. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent; thus do I hold it. ‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so wishes to build a large dwelling for himself, with a patron.
He requests the Saṅgha for the inspection of the site for the dwelling.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the bhikkhus named so-and-so and named so-and-so to inspect the site for a dwelling for the bhikkhu named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk, named so-and-so, desiring to build a large dwelling for himself with a patron,
requests the Saṅgha to inspect a site for a dwelling.
The Saṅgha appoints the monks named so-and-so and so-and-so to inspect the site for a dwelling for this monk, named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable ones approve of the appointment of the monks [named] So-and-so and So-and-so to inspect the site for a dwelling for the monk [named] So-and-so, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monks [named] So-and-so and So-and-so to inspect the site for a dwelling for the monk [named] So-and-so.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent;
thus do I hold this.
Those monks who have been appointed should go there and inspect the site for the monastery.
One must know whether it is with danger or free from danger, and whether it has space around it or lacks space around it.
If it is with danger and lacks space around it,
one should say, "Do not build here."
If it is a site that is free from harm and has space on all sides, it should be announced to the Saṅgha:
"It is free from harm and has space on all sides.

That monk who is building the dwelling, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down in the kneeling position (ukkuṭika) with palms joined in reverence, should speak as follows:
“Venerable sir, I wish to build a large dwelling for myself, with a patron.
Venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha to designate a site for that dwelling.
It should be requested a second time as well.
A third time she should be asked.
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
This monk, named so-and-so, desires to build a large dwelling for himself with a patron.
He requests the Saṅgha to designate a site for the dwelling.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should designate a site for the dwelling for the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This monk, so-and-so by name, desires to build a large dwelling that has an owner and is intended for his own use.
Thus he requests the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for a dwelling.
The Saṅgha designates the site for a dwelling for the monk named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of the designation of the site for a dwelling for the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve may speak.
The site for a dwelling has been assigned by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent.
“I bear this in mind thus.
A place called a "nest" (sārambha) is either the abode of ants, or the abode of termites, or of rats … or of snakes.
… or the lair of scorpions, or of centipedes, or of elephants, or of horses, or of lions, or of tigers, or of leopards, or of bears, or of hyenas;
or the lair of any kind of animal belonging to the animal realm;
or it is dependent on cultivated grain, or dependent on uncultivated grain, or dependent on a slaughterhouse, or dependent on a place of execution.
It is either near a charnel ground, or near a park, or near a royal residence,
or near an elephant stable, or near a horse stable, or near a prison, or near a tavern,
or near a slaughterhouse, or near a street, or near a crossroads.
It is either dependent on a village, dependent on a town, or dependent on a marketplace.
This is called "with conflict.
This is called "without space."
It is not possible to go around it with a cart as it is yoked, nor to go around it on all sides by means of a ladder.
This is called "without a walkway.
It is called "not involving harm to living beings."
It is not the abode of ants, nor does it depend on a path for travel;
this is called "uninjured."
"Provided with a walkway" means it is possible to go around it with a yoked cart, or to go all around it by means of a ladder.
This is what is meant by "provided with a walkway."
A "Mahallaka" vihāra is said to be one that has an owner.
As for the term "vihāra":
It is either plastered on the inside, or plastered on the outside, or plastered both inside and outside.
"Should have it made" means either he makes it himself or has it made by another.
"Or, without having had monks designate the site":

if he builds or causes to be built without having had the monastery site designated by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the effort;
when one brick remains unplaced, there is an offense of grave transgression (thullaccaya).
When that morsel has been brought [to him], there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
"Entailing suspension" ...
[as before] ... for that reason it is called "an offense entailing suspension."

If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site that has not been formally assigned, where harm will be caused, and which lacks space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site that has not been formally assigned, where harm will be caused, but which has space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.

If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site that has not been formally assigned, where no harm will be caused, but which lacks space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site not formally authorized, where harm will be caused, and which lacks a space for walking around, he commits an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site formally authorized, where harm will be caused, and which lacks a space for walking around, he commits two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site formally authorized, where harm will be caused, but which has a space for walking around, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.

If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site that has been formally designated, where no harm will be done to living beings, but which lacks a space for walking around, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a bhikkhu builds a dwelling on a site that has been formally designated, where no harm will be done to living beings, and which includes a space for walking around, there is no offense.
A bhikkhu gives instructions: [text continues]
“Build a dwelling for me.

They build a dwelling for him on a site that has not been formally assigned, where harm will be caused, and which lacks space on all sides; there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). … [omission] … [They build it] on a site where harm will be caused but which has space on all sides;
there is an offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing. … [omission] …
If it is a site where no harm will be done and which lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing together with a *saṅghādisesa* offense. ...
If it is a site where no harm will be done and which has space on all sides, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
A bhikkhu gives instructions: ...
“Build a dwelling for me.

They build a dwelling for him on a site that has been pointed out, where there is encroachment and no space on all sides; there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas* … [and so on] … [where there is] encroachment but space on all sides;
there is an offense of one *dukkaṭa* … [and so on].

If it is a place where no harm will be done and which lacks a surrounding space, there is an offense of wrong-doing. …pe… If it is a place where no harm will be done and which has a surrounding space, there is no offense.
If a bhikkhu departs after having given his instructions, [there is no offense].
“Build a dwelling for me,” he said.
Yet he did not instruct them:
“Let it have its site designated, let it be free from harm to living beings, and let it have a walkway around it.”

If they build a dwelling for him on a site that has not been formally authorized, where there is injury to living beings and no space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
… [omission] … If it is a site where there is injury to living beings but there is space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.
… [omission] … If it is a site where there is no injury to living beings but there is no space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing. … [omission] …
If it is on a site that has not been cleared and lacks space for a walkway around it, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A monk gives instructions and then departs, saying:
"Build a dwelling for me."
And he does not instruct: "Let it have a designated site, be free from harm, and have space on all sides.
They build his monastery on a designated site that involves harm and lacks space on all sides; there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*... [and so forth].

If it involves harm to living beings and lacks space for circumambulation, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) …pe… if it involves no harm to living beings but lacks space for circumambulation, there is an offense of wrong-doing …pe… if it involves no harm to living beings and has space for circumambulation, there is no offense.

"Build a dwelling for me.
And he gives the instruction:
“Let it be on a site that has been pointed out, free from encroachment, and with space on all sides.
But they build his monastery on a site that has not been pointed out, with encroachment, and without space on all sides.
He hears: “It seems my monastery is being built on a site that has not been pointed out, with encroachment, and without space on all sides.”
That bhikkhu should either go himself or send a messenger, saying:
"Let it be a site that has been formally designated, free from harm, and with space on all sides" ...
[or] "Let it be a site that has been formally designated and free from harm" ... [and so forth].
“Let it have a designated site and a surrounding space,” … [and so on] … “Let it have a designated site.
If he does not go there himself or send a messenger, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
A bhikkhu, having given instructions, departs, saying:
"Build a dwelling for me.
And he gives the instruction:
“Let it have a site that has been designated, be free from encroachment, and have space on all sides.
Yet they build his monastery on a site that has been designated, but which involves encroachment and lacks space on all sides.
He hears: “A monastery is being built for me on a site that has been designated, but it involves encroachment and lacks space on all sides.”
That bhikkhu should either go himself or send a messenger, saying:
"May it be free from harm and have a walkway around it.
…pe…
“If it is ‘let there be no starting [of construction],’ and [the monk says] ‘let there be space for walking around,’ there is no offense.”
A bhikkhu gives instructions and departs, saying: "Build a dwelling for me. He instructs:
"Let it be on a site that has been designated, free from harm, and provided with space around it.

They build the dwelling for him on a site that is not designated, where there is harm, and which lacks space around it. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three craftsmen. …pe…
If it involves injury to living beings and lacks sufficient space for walking around, there is an offense of wrong-doing for both craftsmen.
… [and so on] … If it does not involve injury to living beings but lacks sufficient space for walking around, there is an offense of wrong-doing for both craftsmen.
… [and so on] … If it does not involve injury to living beings and has sufficient space for walking around, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the craftsmen.
A bhikkhu gives instructions and departs, saying: “Build a dwelling for me.
He instructs: “Let it be on a site that has been designated, free from harm, and with space on all sides.
They build a dwelling for him on a site that has been designated, but which involves harm and lacks space on all sides. There is an offense of wrong-doing for the two craftsmen … [and so forth] …

If there is harm to living beings and no space for walking around, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the craftsmen … [as above] … if there is no harm to living beings and no space for walking around,
it is an offense of wrong-doing for the craftsmen … [as above] … if there is no harm to living beings and there is space for walking around, there is no offense.
A bhikkhu, having given instructions, departs, saying: "Build a dwelling for me.
They build a dwelling for him on a site that has not been formally designated, where harm will be caused, and which lacks space on all sides.
If he returns while the work is unfinished, that bhikkhu must either give the dwelling to someone else or demolish it and have it built again.
If he should give it to another, or having broken it, have it made again, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and two offenses of *dukkaṭa*.
… [omission] … If it involves injury and has a surrounding space, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and one offense of *dukkaṭa*.
… [omission] … If it does not involve injury and has no surrounding space, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and one offense of *dukkaṭa*. … [omission] …
If it is a site that has not been cleared and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A bhikkhu gives instructions and then departs, saying, “Build a dwelling for me.
They build a dwelling for him on a site that has been designated, but which involves destruction of life and lacks space on all sides.
If he arrives when it is unfinished, that monk must either give the dwelling to someone else or demolish it and have it built again.
If he does not give it to someone else or demolish it and have it built again, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*.
… [and so on] … if it involves new construction and has an open space around it, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. … [and so on] …

If it is without harm to living beings and without a surrounding space, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) …pe… if it is without harm to living beings but with a surrounding space, there is no offense.
If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If one completes what was begun by oneself through others, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If one completes what was begun by others through oneself, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If one completes what was begun by others through others, there is an offense entailing suspension.
There is no offense:
in a shelter, a cave, or a grass hut,
for the purpose of another.
Except for a dwelling place, there is no offense in any case for one who is insane or for a first-time offender.
The seventh training rule concerning the construction of a monastery is finished.
